statement.text: Can a triangle have sides of length 3, 7, and 11? Explain using the triangle inequality.

prompt.question: Triangle inequality: sum of any two sides must be greater than the third side

options.text: Need to check all three conditions first

correct.explanation: Correct! $3 + 7 = 10 < 11$, so triangle inequality is violated
correct.insight: If even one condition fails, no triangle can exist

incorrect.2: This one check is enough to determine impossibility

prompt.question: What does this mean geometrically?
prompt.hint: The two shorter sides can't reach each other when stretched

options.text: No triangle possible: sides 3 and 7 can't connect across gap of 11
Triangle exists but is very obtuse

correct.explanation: Correct! When you place the longest side (11), the other two (3 and 7) can't meet
correct.insight: Think of it as: can you walk 3 steps + 7 steps to cover 11 steps? No, you're 1 short!

incorrect.1: Degenerate happens when sum equals (not less than) the third side
incorrect.2: No triangle can be formed at all when inequality fails

keyInsights: No triangle possible with sides 3, 7, 11 because $3 + 7 = 10 < 11$ violates triangle inequality.
summary.fullSolution: Triangle inequality requires $a + b > c$ for all pairs. Here $3 + 7 = 10 \not> 11$, so no triangle exists.
